pr_title: Add `Parameters#expect` to safely filter and require params
pr_body:
### Motivation / Background

I've been hunting around trying to fix the problem with the default, recommended way of handling parameters in Rails.

```ruby
user_params = params.require(:user).permit(:name, :age)
```

This is fine until someone using your app starts messing with the parameters and causing 500 errors by passing:

```
/path?user=string
```

This causes a NoMethodError because `permit` is called on `"string"`.

The recommendation is not the best way. Instead, the first statement should be written like this:

```ruby
user_params = params.permit(user: [:name, :age]).require(:user)
```

### Detail

In this PR, I propose a new method on ActionController::Parameters that safely handles params filtering in one method, cuts down on ignorable errors caused by params tampering, and improves the specificity of param types.

```ruby
params = ActionController::Parameters.new(user: { name: "Martin", age: 40 })
permitted = params.expect(user: %i[name age])
permitted.permitted?   # => true
permitted.has_key?(:name) # => true
permitted.has_key?(:age) # => true
```

In order to ensure consistent filtering of hashes vs arrays in params, `expect` introduces a new Array matching syntax using a double array `[[:attr]]`. (this example uses shorthand for all but the first example to make it more readable. The hashes returned are actually permitted ActionController::Parameter objects)

```ruby
# Array is expected with `permit`
ActionController::Parameters.new(comments: { text: "Hello" }).permit(comments: [:text]).require(:comments)
# => #<ActionController::Parameters {"text"=>"Hello"} permitted: true>
ActionController::Parameters.new(comments: [{ text: "Hello" }]).permit(comments: [:text]).require(:comments)
# => [{"text"=>"Hello"}]
Parameters.new(comments: { text: "Hello" }).permit(comments: [[:text]]).require(:comments)
# => param is missing or the value is empty: comments (ActionController::ParameterMissing)
Parameters.new(comments: [{ text: "Hello" }]).permit(comments: [[:text]]).require(:comments)
# => [{"text"=>"Hello"}]

# Array is expected with `expect`
Parameters.new(comments: { text: "Hello" }).expect(comments: [[:text]])
# => param is missing or the value is empty: comments (ActionController::ParameterMissing)
Parameters.new(comments: [{ text: "Hello" }]).expect(comments: [[:text]])
# => [{"text"=>"Hello"}]

# Hash is expected with `permit`
Parameters.new(user: { name: "Martin" }).permit(user: [:name]).require(:user)
# => {"name"=>"Martin"}
Parameters.new(user: [{ name: "Martin" }]).permit(user: [:name]).require(:user)
# => [{"name"=>"Martin"}]

# Hash is expected with `expect`
Parameters.new(user: { name: "Martin" }).expect(user: [:name])
# => {"name"=>"Martin"}
Parameters.new(user: [{ name: "Martin" }]).expect(user: [:name])
# => param is missing or the value is empty: user (ActionController::ParameterMissing)
```

As you can see, `permit` will expect an array when the "double array" syntax is used, but defaults to the old behavior of allowing both arrays and hashes otherwise, maintaining backwards compatibility. `expect` on the other hand is strict in for both arrays and hashes.

This pull request also adds the `expect!` method. `expect!` raises an unhandled error in cases where `expect` would raise a handled error that would return a 400 bad request. The unhandled error can be used in cases where it is important to be alerted about a client using incorrect syntax (such as a private internal API where the client should be fixed).

Adds a 400.html template used to render the 400 bad request response.

### Additional information

Related PRs and issues that address this problem:

* Potentially fixes https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/42953 without changing existing behavior.
* https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44297 triggered me to dig into this more, where I arrived at this solution.
* Fixes https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/52463
* Fixes https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/42953

This was what motivated me to create this. It's certainly wrong to return 500 when the client caused the problem, but once `require(:key)` returns the value of `params[:key]` we're in plain ruby land and a `NoMethodError` is bound to occur if you call `permit` next. I think we must just remove all uses or mentions of the pattern `require(:key).permit(:attr)` and switch to this new method. I aim to do that here to the extent possible.

`permit(key: [:attr]).require(:key)` is how rubygems.org now processes _all_ params and it has removed an annoying class of 500s that used to get us paged occasionally. I will to convert to this once it's released.

@martinemde Yeah, global config for logging and raising/ignoring via method call is fine by me and I think makes sense for the broad majority of apps.
What I mean in particular with "does not play nicely" is this case:

```
action_on_unpermitted_params = :raise
# route PATCH /users/1 => users#update
params.expect(user: [:name, :age]) # raises, b/c params contains unpermitted param :id
```
I think at this point, `:raise` basically kills your app and `:log` produces lots of noise. Also in a nested context like `/groups/1/users`, the `create` action also logs/raises.
To improve the situation, one would probably move the actual filtering that `permit` does into an internal method, say, `apply_filters`, and then `expect` could use that, so `unpermitted_keys!` is not called automatically.
Also, `unpermitted_keys!` needs to accept an argument to trigger `:raise` by hand and use global config as fallback. 



On another note, sadly the use case how to replace `params.fetch(:x, {}).permit(...)` is not covered, but I guess this is out of scope for this PR. At least I don't know a good way how to incorporate it.

Also, I would love to make a followup PR to 

1. Account for `action_on_unpermitted_params`
2. enable devs to `:raise` via `*_only`
3. enable the `params.fetch(:x, {}).permit(...)` pattern (maybe this could be named `accept` and `accept_only`, as in, "it is accepted, but not expected").

@dari-us, ok, I understand now what you mean. The fact of how permit works when applied to params "root" means it would consider any other params to be unpermitted. This explains something I was noticing on rubygems.org, which is that dev was logging more unpermitted params than usual.

Possible fix, but maybe too ugly: `id, nested_id, table_params = params.expect(:id, :nested_id, table: [:attrs])`

Edit: thinking ahead about `expect_only`, the way to make attributes required and permitted, while still raising on nested params that are not permitted, you would do: `expect(user: {}).expect_only(:name, :age)`

As for the other methods, I think you're right. The `fetch.permit` pattern could be `allow(user: [:name, :age])` which would return `{}` on missing key. Then it uses the same pattern as expect but communicates that, just like many mocking frameworks, allows might or might not happen and that's ok. (I prefer allow over accept because accept sounds a lot like expect, just transpose a syllable).

@martinemde Actually `expect` and `accept` was intentional as to not confuse it with `permit`, since `permit` and `allow` are kinda samey, but yeah, naming stuff is hard, so I don't know.

I think in order to account for `action_on_unpermitted_parameters`, `expect` (and later on `allow`) needs to iterate each of its keys and call `unpermitted_parameters!` for each sub-hash, f.e.:

```
user_params, group_params = params.expect(user: [:name], group: [:name])
# Here, expect needs to check user_params and group_params each for any unpermitted params and take action

# Maybe something like this
def expect(*filters)
  ...
  values = params.require(keys)
  if self.class.action_on_unpermitted_parameters
    # account for params that were expected on the root level. if none, ignore root level altogether
    unpermitted_parameters!(params) unless values.all? { |v| v.is_a?(self.class) }
    # check all sub-params for unpermitted keys
    keys.zip(values).each do |k, v|
      self[k].unpermitted_parameters!(v) if v.is_a?(self.class) # value could also be a scalar, if so, ignore
    end
  end
  values.size == 1 ? values.first : values
end
```

Same will apply to `expect_only` and `allow_only`, but there `unpermitted_parameters!` is unconditionally called with `:raise`.


Using this technique, `expect_only` would work with the same arguments as `expect`, since it only raises on nested keys and does not care about "root" if no root keys are explicitly expected.

```
params = ActionController::Parameters.new({ id: 1, user: { name: "me", age: "old", leet: "haxor" } })
params.expect_only(user: [:name, :age])
# compares keys of params[:user] with filtered list from args and finds :leet is unpermitted, so it raises
```

I don't know a better solution for params expected on mixed levels (i.e. root + nested, f.e `params.expect(:id, user: [:name])`).
As I see it, there are two cases to consider:

1. Only root params or mixed root + nested: Check root level and each nested params
2. Only nested params: Ignore root level, check each nested params

Not as elegant as `permit.require` under the hood, but without ditching global `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` altogether I see no other way.

@martinemde In my mind, returning either `Parameters` or an `Array<Parameters>` should be considered a bug, read on for a demonstration that clarifies this.
Seeing as `expect` aims to replace the `require.permit` pattern, you have to think like this:
When you `require`, you expect an instance of `Parameters`, on which you then `permit` some scalars, i.e. the end result is `Parameters` with `@permitted = true`.
So there is no way you ever expect `require` (aka the root key) to return an `Array` (or anything other than `Parameters` for that matter).
Translating this into `expect`, `expect(user: [:name])` should be equivalent to what devs expect from `require(:user).permit(:name)` according to the "old" Rails docs.

Here is an executable test case demonstrating, that `permit(user: [:name])` is deficient to account for single instances vs Arrays.
As can be seen below, there are 2 variants of `Parameters` for the `User has_one :bio`, one time with an `Array<Hash>`, one time with a singular `Hash`.
Using the ***same*** filter on both of these `Parameters` returns an `Array<Hash>` for the invalid one for `bio_attributes` (when `Hash` is expected and the only valid option), which crashes when assigning it to `User` instance.

Is there a rationale in the docs for returning either `Hash` or `Array<Hash>` for these kinds of nested permits? Seems really error-prone to me.
Your proposed solution of making it explicit that an `Array` is expected via the use of `expect(user: [[:name]])` seems like a really good solution to me. And yes, I absolutely want to be strict about these things. I want to control, whether a key in `Parameters` points to

1. a scalar
2. nested `Parameters`
3. an `Array`

One caveat, `Parameters.new({ attrs: { "0" => { name: "a" }, "1" => { name: "b" } } })` contains a `Hash` on the surface level, but this actually translates into an `Array`. It is also permissible by `permit(attrs: [:name])`, which explicitly allows numbered Hash keys...
I think, such a structure should also ***only*** be permitted by use of `permit(attrs: [[:name]])`.

And another huge caveat: this is a breaking behavioral change, but is actually needed in order to fix the bug demonstrated by below test case.

Maybe only `expect` and `allow` should behave like this.

```
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3", "~> 1.4"
end

require "active_record"
require "action_controller"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :users, force: true do |t|
    t.string :name
  end

  create_table :bios, force: true do |t|
    t.references :user
    t.text :bio
  end
end

class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one :bio
  accepts_nested_attributes_for :bio
end

class Bio < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :user
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def filter_params(params)
    params.permit(user: [:name, { bio_attributes: [:bio] }]).require(:user)
  end

  def setup
    params_hash = { "user" => { "name" => "itsame" } }
    @invalid_params_hash = params_hash.deep_merge("user" => { "bio_attributes" => [{ "bio" => "it is myself" }, { "bio" => "hello, it's just me" }] }).with_indifferent_access
    @invalid_params = ActionController::Parameters.new(@invalid_params_hash)

    @valid_params_hash = params_hash.deep_merge("user" => { "bio_attributes" => { "bio" => "it is myself" } }).with_indifferent_access
    @valid_params = ActionController::Parameters.new(@valid_params_hash)
  end

  def test_same_filter_ensures_data_integrity_for_nested_attributes
    valid_params = filter_params(@valid_params)
    user = User.new(valid_params)
    assert_equal @valid_params_hash[:user], valid_params.to_h
    assert user.save
    user.reload if user.persisted?
    assert user.bio

    invalid_params = filter_params(@invalid_params)
    user = User.new(invalid_params)
    assert_equal @invalid_params_hash[:user].slice(:name), invalid_params.to_h
    assert user.save
    user.reload if user.persisted?
    assert_not user.bio
  end
end
```

I absolutely recognize the underlying problem here, but I think we've gone a bit off track trying to solve every possible problem permutation, and as a result we've ended up with far too many methods, which leads to much higher conceptual overhead. I don't think that trade is worth it.

I'm willing to add 1 method that captures the require().permit() pattern and deals with the original issue. Everything else should simply raise a parameter exception, which we can capture and discard by default. The annoyance with improper parameter formatting is that it causes noisy exceptions that just don't matter. So the real problem here is how do we get rid of those without harming the development experience,

Here's a quick sketch:

```ruby
class UsersController < ApplicationController
  # POST /users?name=X will raise ActionController::UnexpectedParameter
  # By default, ApplicationController should have
  # rescue_from ActionController::ExpectedParameterMissing, with: -> { head :bad_request }
  def create
    User.create! params.expect(user: [ :name, :age ])
  end
end
```

This should not raise on params being `{ user: { name: "x", age: "20", address: "y" } }`. The only thing that'll cause an unexpected exception is if user is missing. Even `{ user: { name: "x" } }` (where age is missing) should not raise. All we're interested in is getting the first key required, and the subsequent keys permitted, without raising a 500 if that's not right.

Together with this, we should add a default public/400-bad-request.html file.

Only additional method I'd be willing to entertain in addition to #expect is #expect!, which would then raise instead of just swallow the exception. So it would cause a 500 instead of a 400. This might be useful for, say, internal APIs where you really do want to know if a malformed request is being attempted by, say, your own mobile apps.

But we should keep the original mission top of mind otherwise: Get rid of exceptions from malformed requests so that they don't gunk up reporting and alerting pipelines. And we just need to get rid of the majority of it, not necessarily every imaginable case.

@dhh
Thanks for the feedback.
Quick sketch why "adding one method" sadly isn't enough:

```ruby
class UsersController < ApplicationController
  # POST /user?user[name]=me&user[bio_attributes][][bio]=evil&user[bio_attributes][][bio]=haxor

    User.create!(params.expect(user: [:name, bio_attributes: [:bio]]))

```

Another 500 due to param tampering sadly remains unfixed with "keeping everything as it is just adding one method".

Also, it sounds to me, that you want to discourage/deprecate `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` due to the non-descriptive errors it produces, is that correct? Fine by me, just curious.

Again, we don't need to solve all permutations of this problem. We just need to solve the most common ones. Chasing a 100% solution is going to lead to a complicated and hard to understand API in service of edge cases. That's the trade-off I'm not willing or interested in making.

 Yeah, only just see `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` now. Not a fan at all. This is not the kind of setting that should be controlled at the top level, and I also think it's an awkward API in any case. Would like to see that go away.

I want parameter exceptions raised by #expect to be caught and 400 returned. If you want an exception, you can use #expect!. It should be evident at the call-site what happens.

Not gonna argue whether `accepts_nested_attributes_for` is an edge case or not, at least "flat" parameters can be safely `expect`ed then.

Yeah, let's keep this on track, because I absolutely would argue that `accepts_nested_attributes_for` was a mistake, and I'd love to remedy that some day as well 😂. But totally cool to extend what we have in the default box here with a SuperStrongParameters gem or the like that can wrap our basic defaults with a much wider API.

Thanks for the feedback @dhh.

It sounds like I can refocus on getting rid of annoying 500s that should be 400s.

In service of that focus, let's do the following:
1. drop `allow`, since that's focused on optional parameters, a replacement for `params.fetch(:key, {}).permit`.
2. drop the `_only` methods, since those are addressing `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` which is a separate issue.
3. (?) keep the `[[:array, :of, :hashes]]` since that's now much more likely to cause 500s with `expect` syntax. (@dhh absolutely let me know here if I misread your take on this part)
4. (?) do we add `expect!` to raise when the params are given in a bad format? (I'm not sure it's all that different from ParameterMissing, which we will raise from `expect` and you can rescue if needed. In both cases it's a params that is not as expected (both nil and string are the wrong type when a hash is expected))

If we want to consider each of these separately, I can crunch this down to just `expect` and then open a new PR for `allow` and the `only` methods so we don't have to boil the ocean here.

point 3: `expect(user: [:name, :age])` implicitly allows either `{ user: { name: "Martin" } }` or `{ user: [{name: "Martin"}, {name: "DHH"}] }`. If we introduce `expect(user: [[:name, :age]])` for the second case where an array is expected, then the first case can continue to be written `expect(user: [:name, :age])` and only allow non-arrays to match. The catch here is that `permit` allows the same format and we need to decide if we deprecate the old loose matching.

point 4: it sounds like actually we should replace `expect_only` with `expect!` and keep the same behavior as if `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` is true. That's what the `_only` methods do currently

Point 3: I see. I like the disambiguation, but we only apply that to this new method. I don't want to break/deprecate anything on the existing methods. Because, really, going forward, our recommendation will almost always be that everyone should be using #expect all the time. So it's not worth the breakage or forcing function on the past API.

Point 4: That sounds great. I'd actually like for #expect/! to entirely ignore `action_on_unpermitted_parameters`. This is a new API, so we can cut a clean break here. For #expect/!, you'll always be able to tell from the call-site what happens. If you bang, there's an exception and a 500. If you don't, there's a 400.

So we're essentially soft deprecating #permit and #require. Don't want to actually deprecate, and force everyone to upgrade. But in docs and whatever, we just focus on #expect going forward.

Are there any common cases that #expect does not handle where someone would still want or need to use #permit and #require?

Hmm, maybe we're misunderstanding each other. I don't actually think we should have any function that raises when there are extra parameters. I only want one that raises when the required parameter is missing and another that does 400 when that require parameter is missing. So don't think adding #permit! makes sense.

We'll add #expect, which should cause a 400 when the required part of the expect is missing so `expect(user: [ :name, :age ])` results in the 400. Whereas `expect!(user: [ :name, :age ])` results in a 500 when user is missing (but not if either name or age is missing).

@dhh, thank you for clarifying, I think I stumbled over this a little. I closed the PR because it's actually not what we were aiming for. Please ignore the extra noise.

Can you clarify the use case for `expect!`? I imagined it was related to the `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` but it sounds ilke that's unrelated.

From my vantage point, raising `ParameterMissing` allows the user to decide how to behave when the params are malformed for whatever reason. I'm not sure that distinguishing between missing and wrong type is right. Instead, I'd expect people that care about that to rescue `ParameterMissing` and then handle it however they want if they don't want the 400.

EDIT: To put it another way, sure we can produce a 500 from `expect!`, but what should the error be if it's not `ParameterMissing` and should we raise the same error for `user=nil` and `user=string`?

My thinking is this. We're doing all this work to get rid of a bunch of 500s related to malformed requests coming from the world. We generally don't care about folks URL hacking and producing these nonsense requests. We just want to show them a 400. Just like we'll show them a 404, without logging an exception, if they do /users/<id-that-doesnt-exist>.

That's what the new #expect method should largely solve (not withstanding the edge cases on nested assignments, as discussed above). Just throw away malformed requests by serving them a 400 and don't log an exception for it.

Then there's the case where you're not expecting requests from the world. You control the whole chain, and you want an extra layer of protection that you catch any malformed requests, because that means you made a mistake. That to me is the internal API + mobile app case. You control both sides, you don't want malformed requests ignored with a 400. You want a 500, and you want it logged. That's what #expect! is there for.

#expect! should raise a unique exception that's bubbled all the way up, such that it produces a 500, and such that it'll get captured by the likes of Sentry. I don't think we can use ParameterMissing here for that, since we already use that for other cases?

#expect will technically also raise an exception, but we'll have a preconfigured rescue_from that turns that exception into a 400, and doesn't bubble.

Does that make sense?

@dhh, got it. Private/internal API use case explains it perfectly. I can do that.

Should `expect!` also be strict about unpermitted params (extras that shouldn't be there). The new `expect!` is intended to be rather strict about what it receives. In that case I would propose we raise the existing error `ActionController::UnpermittedParameters` when something is there that wasn't permitted, and `ActionController::MalformedParameters` when something is the wrong type. `expect` would just consider malformed to be the same as missing, but `expect!` would disambiguate.

No, I generally don't find strict useful. Who cares what extra stuff is being submitted, as long as you get what you need to process the request. I think we currently have a logging function in development that logs this, which I sorta can tolerate, but even that I often find annoying. So let's just ensure that expect! only raises if you don't get what you asked for (which is the same as what required used to do).

What is required() currently raising? Does feel like it's that which we want.

> What is required() currently raising? Does feel like it's that which we want.

`ActionController::ParameterMissing` which is the same thing `expect` would raise if the params are malformed, and already what is handled by rails as a 400.
Ah, perfect. Then we're good with that. Then it's just #expect! that needs another exception such that it'll produce a 500 instead of 400. Hmm. Maybe `ActionController::ExpectedParameterMissing`?
Alternatively we could keep the same exception but add a flag on it whether to swallow (400) or bubble (500)? Although having separate exceptions is probably easier.

@dhh Your stance on nested parameter assignment is conflicting with what you said in regards to @martinemde Point 3, which is basically the same issue, i.e. clear disambiguation between expecting `Parameters` (`params.expect(user: [:name])`) versus `Array<Parameters>` (`params.expect(user: [[:name]])`), as `params.expect(user: [:name])` with the current implementation of `permit` allows both `{ user: { name: "Martin" } }` and `{ user: [{ name: "Martin" }, { name: "DHH" }] }`, which you said you want to disambiguate.

Solving one but not the other is rather inconsistent IMHO.
@dari-us I think we _are_ including the explicit array format for `expect` and `expect!`.

@dhh, I'll implement this as described. Thank you for clarifying.

I'll come up with a name for the new error and we can change it in review easily.

In summary:
* `expect`: strict about ~~types~~ structure (hash/array/scalar), explicit array format, not strict about excess params that are ignored, raises ParameterMissing which gets picked up and rendered as a 400. Add a 400 html template.
* `expect!`: same as expect, but if a parameter is the wrong type, not just missing, it will raise a new error, somewhat preserving the behavior of permit right now, but raising a better error than `ArgumentError` so it helps fix internal APIs, etc.
Yes, I think that all sounds correct. Thanks for working on this!

I made a fresh fork of rails and applied the changes you made and implemented the methods as requested.
So this should almost be the final thing:
https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...dari-us:rails:params-expect

In summary:
- Removed `expect_only`, `allow`, `allow_only`, `permit_only` and their corresponding tests
- Created `class ExpectedParameterMissing < ParameterMissing; end` intended to be excluded from `rescue_responses` and thus raise 500

I had started down a path of defining a different params processor that detects when we get the wrong type for an expected filter and raises `"'[]' filter expected Array, got Hash"`.

Yours is certainly much simpler, but it blurs missing and malformed. It is very similar to adding `rescue ActionController::ParameterMissing` in your action anywhere you would use `expect!` which doesn't provide any extra information about whether your internal API is being used incorrectly.

If you're amenable, this PR now contains only the `expect` method. We could merge this and then continue with expect! once we have a finalized behavior for `expect`. I think there's still a little confusion.

If all we need is @dari-us' approach, then it's simple to add and @dari-us can simply make an additional PR. If we want to catch and report expected types separately than missing/blank params and not just raise for all of them, then we need a more thorough re-plumbing of the parser. It currently has a lot of places where incorrect types are ignored (it effectively cherry-picks the type it's looking for in almost all cases, ignoring anything else that's incorrect.)

> if a parameter is the wrong type, not just missing, it will raise a new error, somewhat preserving the behavior of permit right now

"Preserving the behavior of permit right now" to me sounded like discarding wrong types without being specific about what went wrong.
So `{ user: { name: "Me" } }.expect(:user)` would produce a message saying, that `user` was missing or empty, i.e. not part of the hash. You want something like `user needs to be scalar, but was Hash`, right? Not sure if this could be simplified to saying `param is missing or the value is empty or unexpected: user`. (EDIT: Now that I'm thinking about it, maybe it makes sense to update also the exception message of regular `expect` to include the `value is empty or unexpected`, as it basically `permit`s first, getting rid of anything unexpected, then `require`s at which point it doesn't know whether the keys originally existed or contained empty/unexpected values. We could make it sensitive to that by exploiting `self[:key]`, but only on the root level, which means for deeper nested keys the distinction cannot be made.)

Only changing the message saves the trouble and complexity of rewriting all filter methods and should hopefully be enough for a dev to investigate the issue. I thought the main benefit of `expect!` is that it is not rescued and turned into a 400, but instead produces a 500.

Of course you can `rescue` yourself, but then again, you could technically also `rescue` all your controller actions instead of using `rescue_from`, but it's more convenient this way.

(Random nitpick: You used "premit", i.e. swapping "r" and "e" somewhere in your documentation)

@dhh Are we on the wrong track here regarding `expect!`?

@dari-us typo fixed, thanks.

Let's come up with some examples where I think `expect!` would trigger an error. I'll use the same shorthand. I think we all understand what is meant.

```ruby
{ user: { name: "martin" } }.expect(:user) # 1 UnexpectedParameter: `:user` expected scalar, got Hash
{ user: { name: "martin" } }.expect(user: [[:name]]) # 2 UnexpectedParameter: `[[:name]]` expected Array, got Hash
{ user: ["martin"] }.expect(user: [:name]) # 3 UnexpectedParameter: `[:name]` expected Hash, got Array
{ user: ["martin"] }.expect(user: [[:name]]) # 4 UnexpectedParameter: `[:name]` expected Hash, got String (?I don’t know?)
{ user: "string" }.expect(user: [:name]) # 5 UnexpectedParameter: `[:name]` expected Hash, got String
{ user: { name: { first: "martin" } } }.expect(user: [:name]) # 6 UnexpectedParameter: `:name` expected Scalar, got Hash
{ user: { name: { first: "martin" } } }.expect(user: { name: [] }) # 7 UnexpectedParameter: `:name` expected Scalar, got Hash
```

So do we go deeply into the params to find unexpected formats? Do we ignore them (sometimes they will be ignored because any nested type mismatches are just silently ignored right now)?

I was also just thinking that expect! would catch and reraise. I hadn't considered distinguishing between missing vs wrong type. I'm skeptical that's necessary.
I think the API looks correctly now. Maybe @rafaelfranca could have a 2nd look.

@dari-us Thank you for thoroughly looking through the commit. I fixed most of the things you mentioned.

I reread @dhh's comments after responding above. `expect!` was mentioned as a way to transition off of `action_on_unpermitted_parameters`.

Correct me if I'm wrong, but therefore `expect!` will always raise on unpermitted params and `expect` will never raise on them. Correct?

EDIT:  `expect!` cannot _always_ raise, because if it raises on root params it will break almost all normal usage. It must still ignore unexpected root params when given a hash otherwise you're forced to do `params.expect(:nested_id, :id, table: [:attrs])` or get a raise. Arguably, this is hairy enough that we could entirely remove this behavior for `expect` and `expect!` and people that want the old behavior can use `permit` carefully to achieve what they want.
I was thinking expect! would only raise if the request is malformed or the root element is missing. Not if there are additional parameters that are not being used.
@dhh, ok. Do both expect and expect! ignore the `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` config? It would just be reserved for `permit` then, which seems fine to me. (Edit: updated to this behavior now)

I re-squashed this into 3 reasonably single feature commits. I'm ignoring `action_on_unpermitted_parameters` for `expect` and `expect!` which is the cleanest solution. `permit` remains available if that behavior is desired (and we can follow up later if we need with a `permit_only` on `expect_only` if people want this feature badly enough.)

Please let me know if there's anything else that needs addressing. I think it's very close, if not actually ready.

To make sure we're all 100% on the same page here:
`expect/!` **only** raises on missing or wrongly typed **root** keys.
1. `{ user: "haxor" }.expect(user: [:name])` raises
2. `{ user: { name: "me" } }.expect(user: [:name, :age])` succeeds
3. `{ user: { age: "100" } }.expect(user: [:name])` succeeds (with empty hash)
4. `{ user: { name: "me" } }.expect(user: [:name, pets: [[:name]]])` succeeds

On a side note, I am not happy about the fact the exception message says "missing or empty" instead of "missing, empty or invalid", since technically it can also raise for non-empty values (example 1). However, since it is internally raised by `require` we cannot tell whether the key was originally given. Don't know if there is an elegant way to raise the same exception class via `require` vs `expect` while keeping the original message of `require` intact.

Parameter missing can happen on type mismatches even before this PR, without `expect`. It just happens less often. I pushed a change to the error message to include "invalid".

Example:
```ruby
ActionController::Parameters.new(comments: { text: "Hello" }).permit(comments: []).require(:comments)
```

@martinemde Good example, I think changing the message is the best way forward. Seeing as `fetch(:key)` can **only** raise on missing key, but not on empty value, the exception message for that is already "too much", as "value is empty" can be ruled out by using `fetch`, and yet it is still mentioned.
So I see no problem in adding another "case" to the message.

issue_context.title: StrongParameters default approach prone to 500: Recommended approach?
issue_context.body:
In the [Rails documentation](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/action_controller_overview.html#strong-parameters), there is a recurring pattern of `params.require(:something).permit(:some, :other, :stuff)` to "fetch" a nested `ActionController::Parameters` with `require`, then `permit`ting its content.
To me, this suggests, that `require` ensures it returns a `ActionController::Parameters`, which it doesn't, as it can return arbitrary non-blank or `false` values.
With a little bit of parameter manipulation, it is possible to produce a 500 by making Rails call `permit` on, say, an instance of String.
It baffles me that [the docs](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/action_controller_overview.html#outside-the-scope-of-strong-parameters) state, while not being a silver bullet, StrongParameters is supposed to cover the most common use cases, and yet, it fails at making arguably the most common use case safe against 500.


To guard against this, one can `params.permit(user: [:name, :age]).require(:user)`, however, once in a nested context, where you have more parameters, f.e. `:id` of a parent record, you always have to explicitly permit them as well, like so `params.permit(:id, user: [:name, :age]).require(:user)` or else a log message / exception will occurr, depending on configuration of `action_on_unpermitted_parameters`.
The `permit`, then `require` approach is clumsy, smelly and un-rails-y to me, so I use the following Initializer to address this problem:

```
# config/initializers/action_controller_parameters.rb
module ActionController
  class BadParameterNesting < KeyError
    attr_reader :key

    def initialize(key)
      @key = key
      super("param must contain nested params, but doesn't: #{key}")
    end
  end

  class Parameters
    # like fetch but raises if value is no ActionController::Parameters
    def nested(key, *args, &block)
      value = fetch(key, *args, &block)
      raise BadParameterNesting.new(key) unless value.is_a?(self.class)

      return value
    end
  end
end

ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.rescue_responses.merge!(
  "ActionController::BadParameterNesting" => :bad_request
)

```

Is there something I am missing or is a monkey-patch like this the only way to make the most common use case of StrongParameters bulletproof against 500?
This is a problem for `params.require(...).permit(...)` and `params.fetch(:x, {}).permit(...)`, which are both solved by `params.nested(...).permit(...)`.
comments:
> With a little bit of parameter manipulation, it is possible to produce a 500 by making Rails call permit on, say, an instance of String.

Can you provide an example of such a request that would produce a 500?

`"something" => "else"` would cause that to raise an error since `something` isn't a hash.

I was pretty sure we had an issue for this already, but could not find it.

The approach mentioned in #51674 works for replacing `require(...).permit(...)`, however, I also often use `fetch(:x, {}).permit(...)`, (f.e. for filter forms on index pages). This is also recommended in [the docs](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/action_controller_overview.html#more-examples) for this use case, so it only makes sense to make sure that kind of problem where a fallback is needed gets solved too. I think `mandate` does not account for this.
